claim: Sarcopenia is the generalized and progressive decline in skeletal muscle mass that is accompanied by reduced muscle strength and reduced physical performance.
source: Sarcopenia is the generalized and progressive decline in skeletal muscle mass that is accompanied by reduced muscle strength and reduced physical performance (Cruz-Jentoft and Sayer, 2019; Heymsfield et al., 2015; Santilli et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cruz-Jentoft and Sayer, 2019; Heymsfield et al., 2015; Santilli et al., 2014) and represents established scientific knowledge about sarcopenia.

claim: Loss of skeletal muscle function significantly increases the risk for impaired mobility, falls, fractures, and morbidity.
source: Loss of skeletal muscle function significantly increases the risk for impaired mobility, falls, fractures, and morbidity (Angulo et al., 2016; Landi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies (Angulo et al., 2016; Landi et al., 2013).

claim: In humans, skeletal muscle is the largest insulin-sensitive tissue in the body.
source: in humans, skeletal muscle is the largest insulin-sensitive tissue in the body
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about human physiology.

claim: Loss of skeletal muscle during aging dramatically increases the risk for sarcopenic obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disorders.
source: its loss during aging dramatically increases the risk for sarcopenic obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disorders (Cleasby et al., 2016; Koster et al., 2011; Srikanthan et al., 2010; Stenholm et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Cleasby et al., 2016; Koster et al., 2011; Srikanthan et al., 2010; Stenholm et al., 2008).

claim: Exercise is the only known intervention to prevent sarcopenia.
source: Exercise is the only known intervention to prevent sarcopenia (Joseph et al., 2012; Law et al., 2016; Mcleod et al., 2019; Rebelo-Marques et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Joseph et al., 2012; Law et al., 2016; Mcleod et al., 2019; Rebelo-Marques et al., 2018).

claim: Mobility disability and polymorbidity can prevent the effectiveness of exercise as a means to counter skeletal muscle functional loss.
source: however, mobility disability and polymorbidity can prevent its effectiveness as a means to counter skeletal muscle functional loss.
evidence: This is an inference based on clinical knowledge about limitations of exercise interventions.

claim: No pharmacological therapeutic interventions to treat or prevent sarcopenia have yet been identified.
source: Pharmacological therapeutic interventions to treat or prevent sarcopenia would be a considerable clinical advance but none have yet been identified.
evidence: This represents the state of knowledge in the field at the time of writing.

claim: With increasing age, muscle fibers undergo atrophy, and the levels of fibrosis and intra-muscular fat increase within and around the fiber bundles.
source: With increasing age, muscle fibers undergo atrophy, and the levels of fibrosis and intra-muscular fat increase within and around the fiber bundles (Akazawa et al., 2017; Brioche et al., 2016; Lees et al., 2019; Mahdy, 2019; McGregor et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Akazawa et al., 2017; Brioche et al., 2016; Lees et al., 2019; Mahdy, 2019; McGregor et al., 2014).

claim: Sarcopenia is associated with loss of mitochondrial activity.
source: Sarcopenia is associated with loss of mitochondrial activity (Andreux et al., 2018; Johnson et al., 2013; Petersen et al., 2015; Picca et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies (Andreux et al., 2018; Johnson et al., 2013; Petersen et al., 2015; Picca et al., 2019).

claim: In a variety of species from rodents to nonhuman primates and humans, the more oxidative fibers are resilient to age-related atrophy.
source: although in a variety of species from rodents to nonhuman primates and humans, it is the more oxidative fibers that are resilient to age-related atrophy (Crupi et al., 2018; Lexell, 1995; Murgia et al., 2017; Pugh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies across multiple species (Crupi et al., 2018; Lexell, 1995; Murgia et al., 2017; Pugh et al., 2013).

claim: At the cellular level, aging is associated with fatty acid oxidation insufficiency and the accumulation of intracellular lipid.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Choi et al., 2016; Koves et al., 2008; Koves et al., 2013).

claim: Age-related changes in mitochondrial energy metabolism, cellular redox, and lipid storage anticipate the onset of sarcopenia in nonhuman primates.

claim: Age-related metabolic changes occur in advance of physical activity decline and frailty in nonhuman primates.
